utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been informed that there is the ability to sit next week during the afternoons from Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. We've made no decision about that, but we'll hear the parties in due course as to desirability of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For reasons that I'll explain later, perhaps this morning, there may be difficulties in filling the week with evidence. We'll do our best to put plans into operation to ensure that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider the matter in due course. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I should say we've now been handed copies of the witness's statements. We'll consider in due course whether any or all of them should be exhibited. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, towards the end of the hearing, you said that your family and your father had been in a camp. You also mentioned the common struggle, the joint struggle, of the Serbs and Croats in World War II against fascism. Since you were active in politics, and in view of the fact that you are an educated man, do you know that all the constitutions of Croatia after World War II until the amendments were passed in 1990 contained provisions prescribing that the Serbs were a constituent nation in Croatia? This applies to all the constitutions, the one from 1945, 1965, and 1974. And do you know that the Serbs lost this status in Croatia only in 1990, with these changes? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. During the war, the Serbs acquired equal status at the Zavnoh meeting, and they had this status in every constitution until 1990, when they lost it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to Zavnoh, this is the anti-fascist council of the Peoples Liberation of Croatia. For those who don't know what Zavnoh is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- of course, you hadn't been born yet, but in our country it was well known that the Zavnoh resolution contained statements to the effect that the Serbs in Croatia had sacrificed themselves to an unimaginable extent, that they loved their country, that they had struggled against the enemy, and that there could be no free and democratic Croatia in which the Serbs did not have full equality, just as the Croats do. Do you know about this Zavnoh resolution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and in the first democratic elections, as they are called, we referred to those decisions and the acquired rights of the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the anti-fascist uprising begin in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official information was that it was on the 27th of July, in a place called Srb in Lika. However, when the new government came to power, this was changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in 1941, the anti-fascist uprising in Croatia started in a place called Srb, which is an area inhabited by Serbs. It's situated in Lika. And then it spread throughout Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need, Mr. Milosevic, to consider where this examination is going. You're asking this witness about events long before his birth. It seems to me -- just let me think. It seems to me that you are claiming relevance to these events in -- for events in 1991. We will need to know what the relevance is and we'll need to consider what the appropriate way of dealing with it is. Your case, so you've told us, is that the Serbs were in fear, that that fear arose partly from events 50 years before, and we will have to decide what truth there is in that. The Prosecution case, of course, is that forces were responsible for crimes committed in and against the Croatian population in the area which we are dealing with. So there is a conflict there which we will have to resolve. But nonetheless, I doubt that there's a great deal of point asking this witness about events 50 or 60 years before. Mr. Kay, again, perhaps you could assist us from the point of view of the amicus on this issue. Really, it's a question of how far can cross-examination properly go. It cannot go that every witness is going to be asked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a great degree of relevance in relation to this matter, but it has limited effect, and Your Honour has stated what the broad issues on this matter are, and they have been canvassed with other witnesses, and indeed this witness, before. So for my part, I don't take objection to Your Honour raising this matter at this stage, because the point is well known and the Trial Chamber Bench has expressed it only a moment ago. My greater concern would be that the accused put his full case in relation to matters and dealt with other matters rather than dealing exclusively with historical matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what has been said, and we will reinforce that ruling. The issue which you want to explore is the fear which you say the Serbs had at the relevant time because of matters which occurred before. You can ask the witness about that fear, but you must do so briefly, and particularly we shall not allow a great deal about the history from this witness, who, as I say, wasn't born then. In due course, we're going to allow both sides to call a historian. You can call a historian too. The Prosecution can call a historian. And that's the appropriate time to deal with these historical matters, not with this particular witness. And what is important is during the time available to you this morning, that you should put to the witness, so he can deal with it and so we may know what your case is, anything you disagree with about what he said about happenings in Western Slavonia and other matters that he dealt with in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you asked about the relevance of this, without extensive explanations, the relevance is that in the late 1980s and early 1990s, this same fascism from World War II rose from the grave, and it was not expressed merely through symbols and rhetoric, the symbols and rhetoric dating back to World War II, but also through widespread pogroms of the Serbian population, of their expulsion from the constitution, illegal arrests, murders, pressure, dismissals from jobs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point that you make. You've expressed it before and we have the point. And in due course, you can call your evidence about it. But you're dealing here with cross-examination of a particular witness, and you should restrict yourself to what that witness has said and what he knows about himself. In due course, as it's been said many times, you can call your evidence about these things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have seen, the witness spoke of things he knows about now, and yesterday he gave clear answers to my questions about camps, torture, mutilation, murder, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, let's not take any further time about this. Let's get on with anything else you've got to put, and if you can finish this witness today -- you have to finish him today, but if you can finish earlier, so much the better. You've already put a great deal to him, but anything else which is relevant to his evidence, you should put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that all of this is relevant. I will put a question to him that relates to the year 1990. We are not speaking of fears but of phenomena that occurred in 1990, not some abstract fears from 50 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area you lived in, nearby, was the biggest concentration camp Jasenovac? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is well known how many Serbs, Jews, and Roma were killed in that camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was well known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you knew and what you learned in school in Croatia, how many Serbs were killed in Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we learned was 700.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 700.000 Serbs killed in a single Ustasha concentration camp alone. Do you know about the event on the 27th of March from a rally of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1990, on the 27th of March, 1990, the time the witness is testifying about, an appeal was issued to the Yugoslav public, saying: We have escaped from one hell. We don't want our children and grandchildren to experience the same evil. We are especially embittered by the knowledge that the independent state of Croatia - we are referring to Hitler's Croatia - was in the historical interests of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this appeal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the event, but not the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the event? Could you tell us that, or remind us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like every year, there was a meeting of the camp survivors in Jasenovac to mark the day when they were liberated from Jasenovac, and this is still happening today. It started again in 1995. And on that day they come together and remember these events, and they always call on the conscience of their fellow citizens to make sure that this will never happen again. This has been a tradition from the 1960s, and it's still going on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since this is not an abstract fear, but it's an event that happened, is the information I have here correct, that in Western Slavonia, in 1991 and 1992, several hundreds of Serbs were killed, several hundreds were wounded, and several thousand houses were torched, and 27 Orthodox churches? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the numbers. You say it's several hundred, which could mean 200, 300, 700.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are your figures, since you are a Prosecution witness? Tell me your figures.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we knew, the information we had, and I'm sure it's not correct, because everything cannot be established yet, over 500 people were killed in Western Slavonia. But it is correct that several thousand houses were blown up or torched, and also a large number of villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that 27 Orthodox churches were torched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of churches. It was the Orthodox church that kept these records. But I know a large number of churches were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what was happening, can it be said that the resistance to this violence was spontaneous from the Serb population in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we could put it like that. The resistance occurred in Okucani, when the Croatian police entered, and there was shooting. The rest of Western Slavonia started the war even before there were such killings and torchings. The killings and torchings occurred during the war and after the war. The commanders of Territorial Defence there started the war. Now, whether that was prompted by the events in Okucani, I don't know, but there were still no great danger to justify the shooting and the attacks that occurred there, because the danger was not such yet. But there was fear and lack of confidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Okucani is a part of Western Slavonia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okucani is in Western Slavonia. They're about 25 kilometres from Pakrac and 45 kilometres from Daruvar. So these are all places within a range of 20 to 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the resistance was justified and spontaneous in Okucani, but until the killing occurs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, that's not what the witness said. You mustn’t misrepresent or take on what he said when he didn't say it. It's your case. I know it's your case, but you adopt it as though the witness has said it when he hasn't. Now what you're supposed to do is put questions, Mr. Milosevic, not make a series of comments. Now, let's concentrate on that. While I'm speaking, Witness 37, can you help us with this: You said 500 people were killed and several thousand houses torched. Were you referring to the Serb people who were killed and the houses torched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I mentioned the 500 killed, I had in mind the battles that were fought. So as far as I know, the civilians and a part of the troops. Though this number is not final, believe me, because the number is -- the number of missing Serbs in Croatia is growing. So I was talking about Serbs. They are still looking for their missing persons, and whom they have lost all trace in the war. So this figure is certainly not final. It is much larger. As for the houses, I was talking about Serbian villages and Serb houses, because in this area of Western Slavonia, about 150 to 160 Serb villages were totally devastated, and this went on from October until about mid -- mid-October 1991 until April 1992. In this period villages were torched and plundered and a part of the civilians who stayed behind were either killed or taken to prisons in Bjelovar, Pakracka Polje, and other places.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. We can't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was saying, from what Mr. May has said, it appears that I didn't understand you correctly when interpreting what you had said in order to ask you my next question, I was saying the attack was in Okucani, where the resistance of the Serb population was spontaneous, and then you said in Pakrac, which is 20 kilometres from Okucani, there were no attacks, but they also organised themselves to put up resistance. Is that what you said? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is how it was in Pakrac, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, and Podravska Slatina, where the Serbs were the first to launch an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when Okucani was attacked, who was attacking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I learnt several days later or the next day, it was the Croatian police that entered Okucani and started shooting in Okucani itself. And then the local Serbs responded, and this lasted for a day or two, with interruptions, because the Yugoslav People's Army came to intervene immediately from Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were attacked, and spontaneously they put up resistance against that attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I was informed from Okucani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is how conflicts in Western Slavonia started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how conflicts in Slavonia started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember an order of the Crisis Staff of Slavonska Pozega referring to measures of ethnic cleansing of Western Slavonia, which needs to be cleansed of Serbs? The order of the Crisis Staff of Slavonska Pozega ordering resettlement of 24 Serb villages in the north-western part of the municipality of Slavonska Pozega. Do you remember that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the order. Later on I personally saw it. I remember when the people from those villages partly went towards Slavonska Pozega, and a part of the population who had no confidence in the government went to the area which was at the time under the control of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the purpose of explanation, was there any reason except ethnic cleansing to give the order for the Serbs to be resettled from 24 villages of the municipality of Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequent events showed that there was no cause or reason for this because those villages, with the departure of those people, were burnt down and looted. A part of the population that stayed behind were killed. And just this year their bodies were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this order, which you yourself said had no reason to be issued, there was no reason to throw out the Serbs from 24 villages, does it remind you of the well-known order signed by Kvarternic in 1941 on the 7th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's pure comment. It doesn't matter what it reminds anybody of. That is your argument. It's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a matter for argument. It's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the order is identical to the order of 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can make the point to us if you want. It doesn't matter what the witness's view about it. What you're trying to do is to argue your case through the witnesses, and that's not permissible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In my examination, I'm just endeavouring to have the witness tell me whether something is correct or not, Mr. May, and I think I'm allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the largest number of settlements or the greatest amount of violence - I'm sorry - was manifested in Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Nova Gradiska, Novska, Orahovica, Pakrac, Podravska Slatina, Slavonska Pozega, and Virovitica? These are all the names of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the question be more specific? What kind of violence, by whom, and against whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against the Serbs by these forces of the Croatian authorities. I'm talking about ethnic cleansing, killings, detentions, torture, all types of violence, expulsions, evictions. Was the violence most intensive in this part of Western Slavonia and in the municipalities I have listed? You are familiar with all of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, from August until December 1991, the Serbs, who held their positions, those positions were outside of town; therefore, Daruvar and Pakrac and Grubisno Polje as towns, and Virovitica and Slavonska Pozega, and Orahovica and Podravska Slatina and Novska and Nova Gradiska, they were all under Croatian control. The events were such that in those towns, Serbs were taken to prison and some were mistreated, beaten, some in Novska, Pakrac, and Daruvar were also killed, as happened in Vucin, Cetekovac, and Balinci, and Bucje, where Serbs were in control, similar events occurred. Later on, the exodus of Serbs started from Grubisno Polje and Daruvar - I'm now talking about municipalities as opposed to towns that I mentioned before. These were parts of territories consisting of Serb villages, and with the departure of Serbs from those villages, the villages were devastated and burnt down. And I will repeat what I said: Those who stayed behind were arrested, and after released, and some were killed. So that this area, if we go from the north, from Virovitica, Podravska Slatina, the part of the Serb villages that were in the mountains up to the approaches to Pakrac, which was under the control of the territorial forces and the JNA, were devastated. The villages were totally destroyed, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the events that disturbed the public when, on the Orthodox church in Grdzevci, a large slogan appeared saying "Death to the Serbs"? And then on the 13th of August 1991 already, the Black Shirts arrived, members of the national guards from Virovitica, under the command of an official of the HDZ, Stojan Gustin. This was on the 13th of August, 1991. And then the misdeeds that occurred, do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with these singly. First of all, what is put is that a slogan appeared on a church, "Death to the Serbs". Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was even referred to in its issue of the 19th of July, 1991 by a local newspaper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says he doesn't remember. So the next point is that the Black Shirts arrived, National Guards. Did you see any Black Shirts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't there, and I didn't see that. I did hear that some forces had arrived, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know anything about this event, that is, the arrival of this group of killers of the National Guards, under the command of Stojan Gustin on the 13th of August, 1991, and the misdeeds committed by them? Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this around the 15th of August, and that conflicts broke out which spread later on, but I don't know exactly how it all started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember, for instance, within the context of that event - let me give you a specific example, because hundreds of Serbs were killed on that occasion. Mladen Kekerovic, the wealthiest Serb from Grubisna Polje, and his address Novi Put BB, was arrested, of course without a warrant, by the National Guards, as he was on a business trip and he had money on him. Then they cut off one ear. And when they had seized all his property, they allowed him to leave Croatia. Do you remember that incident at least?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, there were very many events and stories of that kind. I truly do not remember that particular name, but I do know that there were interceptions and people beaten up, but it's a long time ago, so I'm afraid among the host of data, I don't remember that particular name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is what I have here correct or not? Just tell me yes or no. That during the ethnic cleansing, according to data, up to the 15th of August, 1992, in that area, 183 villages were totally ethnically cleansed and 87 partially. Are those figures correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is not quite as many, not quite 183. I think it is a little less, about 170, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not 183, but how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally ethnically cleansed. According to our data, about 165 villages were totally destroyed, and about 50 partially destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when was that, Witness C-037? I think you've told us, but you can remind us again. During what period did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these events began at the end of September and beginning of October 1991 and went on until mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say October. I have information here that, for example, in the municipality of Virovitica, the Croatian forces and armed citizens shot at Serb houses already in early September 1991. Is this true or not? Please just say yes or no so that we don't waste time. I gave you a specific piece of information, the village of Nova Cabuna, the beginning of 1995, so September, not October, armed Croatian civilians and civilian forces shot at Serb houses. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact period. I did hear about that event. This was outside of the control of the area where I was living. We heard also about the village of Kip that this is what happened, and also in the area of Daruvar. So this did happen right after August, so that this time period that you're talking about, September, is probably right, but I don't know exactly anything about this village. I don't have the precise information. I don't have any records so that I could talk about specific dates. But this was the time period when these events began to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about the exact date, but was it the beginning of September?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please tell me now: Since I'm looking at data now which was gathered until the 15th of August, 1992, so only until the 15th of August, that the following villages or settlements have been completely cleansed Bastajski Brdjani, Batina, Batinska Rijeka, Bijela, Donja Vrijeska, Donje Cjepidlake, Gornji Borki, Dobra Kuca, Gornje Cjepidlake, Gornja Vrijeska, Gornji Borki, Katinac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't deal with this, reading out a long list. He can't possibly begin to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list is very long, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can you remember the names of all these 165 villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot remember them all, but the villages that are being cited now are villages in the area of the municipality of Daruvar. But I cannot remember at this moment all of the villages, all of their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've got the general point that it's 165. Now, we don't need to go into any more detail. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I said that it was 183 villages, and the witness confirmed 165 villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we rely on is not what you say. It's what the witness gives in his evidence. That's what the Court relies on. Can we move on from this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in Croatia, from 1991 - and now I'm talking about Croatia, not only about Western Slavonia - that the Croatian authorities blew up 10.000 houses belonging to Serbs, even the occasional Croatian house, where they were owned by people who disagreed with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've given evidence about Western Slavonia. Can you give evidence about what happened in the rest of Croatia or not? Something you read in the paper, then it's of no value really, or something you heard on the radio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I heard about this piece of information in the media, and I heard it talked about in the Croatian different bodies. They discussed the blowing up of these houses. And there was also discussion about that in Strasbourg. But I don't have official information about that, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't hear you, but it sounds what you're saying is irrelevant. There's no point asking a witness what he heard on the radio about facts which can be established by other evidence, if they are facts. What you're trying to do is to argue your entire case through this witness, which is a waste of the Court's time. Ask him about Western Slavonia, by all means. He knows about that, but simply he's read something in a paper, it's of no use to anybody, particularly these general points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, during the examination-in-chief, the examination-in-chief, I expected you to make such a remark to the other side, because to many questions: How do you know about this?, the witness replied that he had seen that in the newspaper or had heard about it on Croatian television. I did not ask in any of my questions for him to say what he had read in the papers. I'm only asking him what he knows. If you look at the transcript of the examination-in-chief, you will see how many times he had said that he had read something in the Croatian press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, did you see the prison in Knin, for Croats, or any camp in Udbina, which you mentioned in the examination-in-chief? Or did you hear about this or read about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Heard about it. So you accept the testimony about something that he had heard and talked about during the examination-in-chief, but you are asking me to ask him only about things that he knows. But he occupied a post in which he was supposed to know things like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will rule and see what value there is in anything which the Prosecution called in evidence, if you're right about that. I don't recollect it, but if you're right we will certainly do that. It's of no point saying I heard on the radio that so many houses were burnt down or whatever, unless he's got some particular connection with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A while ago we established during this questioning his claim about 165 villages, so let us go on. I'm talking about Western Slavonia now. So you won't allow anything else other than Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you please tell me: Is this information correct? Because, for example, I took this information from American -- the American media, Tomislav Mercep, who was the advisor of the minister of internal affairs and a member of parliament, led death squads and a vast number of Serbs were killed by him in Western Slavonia. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from people that -- mention his name, both from Croats and from Serbs, also by some Croat officials that he led actions in Western Slavonia. At that time I didn't have any direct contacts with him, nor did I meet him. His name is linked with villages around Novska which were destroyed and his name is also linked to the Pakracka Poljana. I heard about that, but I don't have any concrete arguments about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And now, since you are living in Croatia, are you aware about the recognition of an officer -- the admission of an officer of his who admitted that he had slaughtered 72 Serbs, officer Bajramovic, and those victims including eight -- no, nine women? Did you hear about this affair and the revelation of these facts relating to Western Slavonia regarding these cruel murders of Serbian civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about this in the newspaper. I read Mr. Bajramovic's interview about these events. And then I know that he was detained and that an investigation was launched against him, and another two persons, that later they were freed due to lack of evidence. And now these proceedings are before the Court again, but without Bajramovic, because he's on the run. But the other two whom he mentioned while he was in investigative detention, in prison, are on trial and they talked about the massacres and murders of Serb civilians in Pakrac, including women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain that Croatia, a state with a rule of law, frees because of lack of evidence a man who himself admits -- Very well. And do you know the activities of Mercep in Vukovar regarding the murders of Serbs, together with Glavas and Seks and their death squads, murders, blockades, and so on? Do you know anything about the activities of Mercep, Glavas, and Seks in Eastern Slavonia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about those things later from Serbs who lived in that area, but I don't have any detailed information about that other than stories that this is what he took part in, that he took Serbs away, he liquidated them, they were dumped in the River Drava. But as I say, I do not have any direct information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, direct information. Yesterday we dealt with a series of issues that I put questions to you about regarding -- which you also said you don't know anything about that. We mentioned a lot of things that you don't seem to know anything about. Do you know -- well, you were in Croatia throughout that period. You listened to their radio and television. Do you know what the Yugoslav National Army was called? I'm asking because I have an order here relating to reporting from combat areas where it is stated: "Not to call the JNA anything else but the Serb or communist occupying army." So during the time that the JNA was in the Croatian part of the Yugoslav territory, the Yugoslav army, it was proclaimed to be the Serbo-Communist Occupational Army, in accordance with orders given to their media. Was this the vocabulary, the terms, that were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vocabulary used was Serbo-Communist and Serbo-Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, relating to Serbo Chetnik, I saw in the report about the questioning of Miro Bajramovic, that he explained that there was no problem for him to cut the throats of women and so on because he wanted to kill them all. As far as we were concerned, they were all Chetniks, and then things just went on automatically from there. So please tell me, since you talked about this yesterday, about the ways in which Serbs were tortured in camps and prisons. Since I have a report here which, based on the examination of a number of prisoners who were exchanged, and these examinations were conducted by the institute for mental health of the military hospital in Belgrade, and it was signed by Colonel Dr. Bratislav Petrovic himself. So this analysis of medical and psychological examinations by experts of these people who came from these camps, is this something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going a long way from what the witness can deal with. Now, time is limited. He gave evidence, for instance, that he was arrested, charged with treason and espionage, detained for 72 days in Belgrade. These are all matters which he's given evidence about. Not a word of cross-examination by you. And there comes a limit to the amount of cross-examination we can allow on the -- what you know now is called the -- or is referred to as the tu quoque basis, that means attacking the other side for the crimes they committed. Now, you're on trial here for various crimes and evidence is being given against you. Now, if you challenge any of the evidence which this witness gave, such as what I've described already, then you must do so, because it's your duty to challenge his evidence rather than put your own case accusing the others of various other crimes, which may not be relevant in the trial. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there's anything you want to ask about that, you should. You should deal with the crimes which it's alleged were committed by the TO and others. These are all matters that you should deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, let's just be clear about one thing. My case is not what you say, the tu quoque case, because Serbia did not commit this. You are talking about a civilian -- civil war in Croatia. To me, who was the president of Serbia, and not the president of Croatia or Yugoslavia at that time, and Serbia was not at war with Croatia and did not commit these things. We have established during the cross-examination of this witness also that all the units who were there that he's aware of were local ones and that Serbia did not take any part in this. So my case is not that you also committed that, but I'm talking about the fact that this has no material or legal basis in order for it to be discussed like this. How can I know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you've established so far, or what you're attempting to establish, as far as I can see, because your evidence is -- or the cross-examination is purely directed to this, is that during this conflict in Croatia, crimes were committed against the Serbs. Now, that may or may not be so, but you must understand it is of limited assistance to us in deciding whether crimes were committed by you and others, as alleged, in Croatia at this time. Now, the witness's evidence is aimed at directing allegations that you, not you personally, but others were involved in these crimes, and you should be concentrating your defence, if I may say, and your cross-examination, in challenging what he says, not simply rehearsing at great length and, if I may say, with much repetition, that crimes were committed against the Serbs. You understand that, that the trial has got to concentrate on the matters of the indictment, not simply on allegations against the other side. It may be that it can concentrate on more relevant issues. And in my view, much too much time has been taken up with allegations against the other side. I speak for myself, of course, but that is my view.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wish to remind you, since I am not concealing my view, that what you call an indictment is a false indictment, for primarily two reasons: First of all, because there was no aggression. It was a civil war. That's the first reason. And the second one is that the Serbian people had this war imposed on them, both in Croatia and in Bosnia, and that for them it was a war of defence. So it is evident that the Serbs were defending themselves on the territories on which they lived, defending themselves from pogroms, such as had been perpetrated 50 years before. That's all I'm saying, Mr. May. That's the only truth I'm trying to explain here. Far be it for me to say tu quoque, because I have committed no crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You challenge, for instance, that this witness was arrested, as is --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The matters related to arrests and such things were discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no need to go into any further detail as to the persecution of Serbs, the ethnic cleansing, and so on, because there is no doubt that this was widespread and covered almost all of the territory; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are speaking of later events, if you're speaking of 1995 and the exodus of the Serbs from the RSK, as it was, then it became widespread, but as for Western Slavonia, I have told you how many villages, municipalities, and people went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said 165 villages and so on. Was this widespread or not, in relation to such a small area as Western Slavonia? Because 165 villages, as you say - I say it's more - would that be widespread or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think it's widespread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many houses did you say were torched or blown up with explosives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going over the same ground again and again. Now, have you got anything else, anything new to ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The amendments, as we concluded, caused people to be upset, but as far as I can remember, after this a discussion was held on preparations for a new constitution of Croatia; is that correct? The amendments were enacted in the middle of the year, and towards the end of the year there were preparations and there was debate about a new constitution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, you took an active part in all this, putting forward proposals, and you took part in the preparation of some amendments on behalf of the political organisations you were active in, which advocated certain rights for Serbs which should be provided for in the constitution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct - and this is my question to you now - is it correct that the Croatian authorities did not take into account a single one of the Serb amendments to the proposed constitution, especially as regards demands that in the new constitution the Serbs should keep their previous status, that is, the status of a people, which they had had in all the previous constitutions ever since the Republic of Croatia came into existence? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, then, the series of laws that deepened or exacerbated the repetition of the system of 50 years before? For example, the law on public holidays. Let me not speak of the Serbs, for example, but the Jews would have the right to an official holiday only if they were members of the Jewish community, and if they weren't, they wouldn't have the right to an official holiday, and so on and so forth. And the Croats could celebrate Christmas for two days, while the Serbs could celebrate it for only one day. So discriminatory laws were enacted in all areas of life, for example, education, the Academy of Arts and Sciences. Do you remember the law on the academy saying that the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences was the legal successor of the Yugoslav academy from 1941 to 1945? This was the academy that had been set up during the fascist government. And there were a number of laws. I cannot quote them all now. Didn't this exacerbate - in parallel with the preparations for the new constitution and the new constitution - didn't it exacerbate the situation in which the Serbian people in Croatia were threatened, imperilled, at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the enactment of these laws, but as for the academy, I don't remember that. It doesn't mean it didn't happen, but I cannot remember that, since you asked about this specifically. But as for public holidays and other things, I remember that, yes, and I know that this caused tension, that people lacked confidence, that they felt discriminated against, so they did not trust the new authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume - and please confirm whether this is correct, in view of the feelings you had then and your relations then - when I say "you," of course I'm not referring to you personally, but to the Serbs. Were you upset by the fact that demands for the Serbian people to retain their previous status in the Republic of Croatia were rejected? I'm referring to the status of an equal nation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did have a negative effect on us. It increased the mistrust, the lack of confidence, because we wanted Croatia to be a civil state, not a national state of the Croats, but a state of all its citizens, and this proposal saying that we were no longer a constituent people really caused the Serbs in Croatia to lack confidence in the new government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After all the events that we have mentioned in this examination, did this not show that the lack of confidence in the new authorities was not unjustified; but on the contrary, that unfortunately, the fears were justified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, all the events that happened after 1995 showed that the fear was justified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall skip over some questions in order to save time, but there is one that I cannot leave out. Do you remember that the law on primary education does not provide for education for children of Serb nationality but only education in the Croatian language, also the law on secondary schools education, while the law on education of minorities provides only for minorities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that the Serbs were not referred to, that they were not given even the status of a national minority? Is this correct, Mr. C-037?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there had been a law on minorities up to that point, which was not -- declared not in force. The Serbs were declared a minority, but there was no law on the basis of which they could realise their rights in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When all this is borne in mind, the constitution, the laws, the violence, the ethnic cleansing, the murders, can it be concluded that the Croatian authorities incited not only nationalism in Croatia but also fascism and discriminatory and insulting stance towards the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are all conclusions which you are asking us to draw. They're not a matter for the witness. You can ask him what the law was and how it was changed, but comments upon it are not for him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a comment, Mr. May, because I am talking about the consequences this had, unfortunately tragic ones, which the witness is testifying about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the election campaign in Croatia - let me be more specific - which illustrates all this, that the election campaign at the beginning of 1990, when it was gaining momentum, intimated, without any question, the attitude of Croatian nationalist parties towards Serbs and their status in Croatia, and after that, this was fully reflected during the preparation for and adoption of the new Croatian constitution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the speeches that were held nationalist, containing threats, an insulting attitude towards the Serbs, which was later materialised through the laws and constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember the HDZ programme adopted in 1989, at its founding assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details any more, but I do know that a programme was adopted, but I cannot talk about the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the details. I'm asking you about the position they took towards all these key issues that I have put to you. Was all that based on this programme adopted in 1989?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come to adjourn. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. There will be another short adjournment later in the morning. We will finish at 1.00. Mr. Kay, if either you or Mr. Tapuskovic got any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There will be a few questions, but it will be under ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but not more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, in the course of your examination, or apart from it, I wonder if you can help us with an issue raised by the accused in the form of general objection to the Prosecution's exhibit regarding, in particular, tab 7 and tab 12 of Exhibit 327. Tab 7 is a minute or a report of a meeting purportedly presided by this witness, but the witness said he doesn't know of this. But I note -- I noted that that very document was attached to the written statement, so he might have said something different at the statement. And tab 12 is a document named as "List of crimes made by the Republic of Croatia, department of war crimes." We admitted it on the ground that it is a prima facie official document, but if you look at the original B/C/S version, it is a typewritten one and there's no official seal, nor anything like that. So if you could deal with this matter or give us your observation. And also for the Prosecution, if you could give us your explanation as to the authenticity of the document or how the Prosecution did get this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An administrative matter. We've reviewed the position of witnesses. We are already facing considerable difficulties arising from the failure so far for waivers to be granted, in particular, cases where witnesses require them. I'm pursuing the problem with all energy, but we may be turning to the Chamber for assistance fairly soon, so that's going to disturb the order of witnesses in any event. As far as next week is concerned, the possibility of sitting three half days next week, obviously we will take any time that's available whenever we can and we will do our best to fill such a week if that time is available. We think we can probably just about get witnesses in, but it will necessarily be again with the consequences of some disturbance of the order of witnesses. What we will do is notify the Court by the end of today, or the accused by the end of the full day, what witnesses we are in a position to call next week, and hope that the Chamber will allow them to be called out of order. For personal reasons, I shan't be here on Monday afternoon or on Tuesday until about 10.00. I hopped to take a witness on Monday morning, I still hope to do so, leaving supervision of cross-examination to one of my colleagues, of course. But if that's still possible, I'd be grateful to start at 9.00 on Monday so ensure I can finish him by the time I have to leave. I had budgeted on 9.00 until 2.00, or 9.00 until 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll do the normal hours for Monday. Tuesday and Wednesday we'll sit in the afternoon, 9.30 until 4.15. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood now that the opposite party intends to change the order of witnesses once again. It seems to me that we had cleared up the matter, that it was the least that could be done for me to have the order of witnesses at least one week in advance. Let me remind you that one thousand twenty-five [as interpreted] thousand pages were disclosed, 600 videotapes, and 200 or 300 audiotapes, and it is absolutely impossible, physically, not to review all this material, but even to make some sort of a selection unless you know at least a few days in advance when which witness will appear. And if the other party wishes to use these tricks, I cannot understand that this is permissible. I think it is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're wrong to talk of tricks. The difficulties arise because of getting witnesses here. We are conscious of the amount of material which has been served on you and the difficulty which you have in preparing your defence, and it's a matter which we keep in consideration. But the order of witnesses is not in fact necessarily set in stone, and occasionally there must be changes. What we have to do is to ensure that you have time for preparation of each, and that we will do. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing I really need to at to the summary of our position that Your Honour has identified. We are of course in many ways entirely in the hands of others. But what I can say is this: Aware of the possibility of the need for future and further changes to the order of witnesses, we will be voluntarily disclosing material earlier than might otherwise have been the case to ensure that the accused has the maximum amount of time to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it may be of assistance, with any changes there is in the order, that he gets, besides the notification, he also gets the witness statement and also the summary, although he's had them before, but if he can have them again so he doesn't have to look for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've already made arrangements for that to happen in respect of changes for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. C-037, can it be said that the civil war in Croatia was initiated by illegal paramilitary formations of the secessionist regime in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What regime are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one who carried out the secession of Croatia by force and contrary to the provisions of the constitution, as of 1990, following the elections.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer in that way, that the war started by the secessionists. I think it broke out due to nationalism, mistrust, incidents, and then the conflict spread. So there was a gradual development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware -- were you aware then, or now, do you know now, that at the beginning of 1990, for instance, the Croatian leadership planned the formation of an armed force, about 44.000 strong, in peacetime, and 220.000 strong in wartime, as preparations for the forcible secession and the expulsion of Serbs from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with such details. I know that there was reference to the formation of a Croatian army, the ZNG was formed. But I do -- I am not aware of any plans, nor did I see them, for the expulsion of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned the national guards corps, the ZNG. That was counter-constitutional, was it not, to form such a guard corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, and really, I'm unable to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time, illegal arming started in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it first from the media, and later I saw civilians being armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When later did you see civilians armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them at the end of May/beginning of June, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that trailer trucks with weapons were illegally delivered and the first arrived on the 12th of October, 1991, and then the next convoy -- I'm sorry, on the 20th of October, 1990 [as interpreted] from the DDR, that is, from the former stocks of the former East Germany.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from the media, but I didn't see that. I heard about it from the media and I heard people talking about it, citizens, discussing this, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of weapons being brought in from Panama, Frankfurt, by planes, also illegally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it was illegal, I couldn't be aware of it. If it had been legal, again I wouldn't have seen it, because I wasn't in such organisations that had access to such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 13th of January, 1991, that is, after the decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia on the disarming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless this witness was involved in this matter, again, you are putting very generalised matters to him which he cannot give evidence about. You have the opportunity to call evidence about them, and you can -- if there are witnesses who can deal with them for the Prosecution, you can cross-examine them. But merely putting your entire defence, your broad brush allegations, and asking witnesses who know nothing about them is of no assistance to us. We have to decide what the limits of this are. Ask him a question he might know something about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him whether he knows about it, Mr. May. I cannot know in advance, like the opposite party, what he does know, nor can I give him the indictment to learn by heart, as the other side has done, to quote from it. He is a Prosecution witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: An improper allegation by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember the confiscation of a Boeing 707 from Uganda full of weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this sort of thing? Were you involved in confiscating a Boeing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I heard about it from the information media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, since a moment ago you said you saw weapons being distributed to civilians and so on: From the standpoint of the strengthening of repression and dictatorship in Croatia, the formation of paramilitary units organised by the ruling political party, that is, the HDZ, the formation of the national guards and their illegal arming and equipment, does that have special significance for the beginning of the civil war in Croatia which was prompted by the persecution of the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his evidence about it. He can't answer these questions of that sort. They are matters which we may have to decide, but this witness can't help us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember, as this was common knowledge in Yugoslavia, that the Presidency of Yugoslavia, in full composition, at a session on the 7th and 8th of May, 1991, which was also attended by the prime minister of the federal government, who was from Croatia, Ante Markovic, as well as the presidents of the presidencies of all the republics, that they adopted a conclusion to form immediately a parity group consisting of representatives of the Republic of Croatia and the legitimate representatives of the Serb people in Croatia for initiating talks on all disputed matters, the main ones being the constitutional equality of the Croatian and Serb peoples, the language, the alphabet, et cetera, et cetera? That was within the context of the things that you were involved in, that is, the so-called Serbian amendments to the Croatian constitution. Do you remember this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Do you remember the decisions to block all barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Croatia on the basis of a decision of the leadership in, in the second half of August, 1991, and the decision to attack them, as well as all units of the JNA, on the 14th of September, 1991? Do you remember those decisions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of those decisions, but I cannot tell you exactly from which sources. I do remember those decisions, because they were widely discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard of the decisions and you remember that such decisions were made, but do you remember the actual practice, what was actually done pursuant to those decisions, that is, the blockade of barracks, attacks on members of the JNA, at a time when Croatia was a legitimate component part of the territory of Yugoslavia, their attacks on the army of Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tell us, witness 37, what you saw or heard yourself, not what you may have heard on the radio what was happening in X, Y, and Z. But tell us what you saw, if anything, of what is being put to you here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was not close to a single barracks, and I was not in a position of seeing any such blockades. I heard about them and I saw it on television and learnt about them from the media. I was not in a position to personally witness these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that refugees, in large waves, set off in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started, one can say, in waves. Whether they were large, I said in reference to Grubisno Polje, between 3.000 and 5.000 people, then later on 15.000, those were the figures of people leaving Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason for them to leave was the pressure of the Croatian forces against them. That surely is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question yesterday, that at the time there were no large concentrations of forces in the area, but there was a developed awareness among the people that they were alone, they were weak, they lacked the strength to defend themselves, and with the commanders of the TO and with the retreat of their families, they left the area, which, as I said yesterday, was subsequently devastated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just look. Because of the limited time, I cannot show you the films and documents, but, for instance, are you aware of facts referred to in this document, for instance? It is a report of the United Nations, the command of sector West. So Sector West was your sector, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It is a report on crimes committed against the civilian population in Western Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the Sector West, Safe Area of the United Nations, and this was a report compiled by the UN. Do you remember that report? It is one particular report signed by Musali on behalf of the commander of the Sector West. And it says, for instance, that in the village of Paklenica, the property of Mr. Solaja, people were slaughtered: Mica Teodorcevic, a veteran without a leg from the village of Paklenica; Nikola Vojnovic; Milan Brdjac [phoen] wounded; Aleksa Raus, a nurse; Senka Raus, a nurse; Ruza Solaja, a nurse; Dusan Hasura, from the village of Rajici; Mitar Vujakelja [phoen], who was wounded in the head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you assist the Court as to these matters? Do you know anything yourself of your direct knowledge, anything about them, Witness C-037?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I heard of these events, but I didn't have occasion to see that report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you see, even nurses had their throats slit, according to the report of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, do you want us to have that report? We haven't got it now. Maybe the Prosecution have got a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm not aware of this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't know about this report. Well, Mr. Milosevic, if you want to put the report in, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could put in lots of such reports, so do admit it. There's no problem in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, do you have any knowledge about a report of Sector West, for the department for civil affairs, for instance, this one? All these things must exist in the original in the archives of the United Nations organisation. This is Sector West, the civilian police, UN, station Okucani. "On the road to Novska we saw many terrible scenes, at least 50 corpses along the road. They were Serbs, soldiers, and civilians. Many houses were destroyed, shelled," et cetera. Do you remember those reports? Or, for instance -- or, for instance, a report just for your sector. We also have the Dalmacija-Zagreb-Gorni Koviljaca-Baranska sector. But just for the Slavonian eparchy a report of the church, 39 churches, 35 parochial homes destroyed in the eparchy of Slavonia, and 40 churches damaged, 15 parochial homes and the eparchy residence in Pakracka destroyed. Did you have this report? Did you ever learn anything about this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you seen that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't seen that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the way to get this evidence before us is to hand in the reports. Now, just help us with this: What is the church report that you've been quoting? Which church and what date, if you please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report of the Serbian Orthodox Church in the Republic of Croatia, the state of church facilities after the expulsion, according to data of the Serb Orthodox Church. That's the report. And the other reports that I quoted from about the cutting of throats of nurses and veterans without a leg, and other victims, these are reports from the United Nations, the command of Sector West of civilian affairs and Sector West civilian police of the station Okucani. This I just happen to have here with me right now, but if you are interested in the truth, you could get all of those reports for you to find out what was going on. Because at least the sources of the UN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will get those reports, but --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these can be entered as exhibits, these two reports here that I have provided. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the usher get those and we'll have a look.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are in B/C/S. We will hand them to the -- we'll hand them to the Prosecution. We will then mark them for identification. They can be translated. And perhaps the Prosecution, certainly in relation to the UN reports, could get the full reports that are being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As soon as we have these documents, we will check whether we have a full version of this document within our vault and see whether we can provide the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be convenient now to give them numbers. The UN report can be the first one, and the church report the second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the UN report will be marked for identification as D41 and the church report will be marked for identification as D42.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to hear your comments about information that I have here from the UN KRO political and humanitarian affairs, the sector of Daruvar, and I have the municipality of Pakrac here, which shows, according to the different settlements, a comparison before April 1991 and October 1995. For example, Batinjani, before April 1991, 154 Serb citizens, 55 Croats; in October 1995, Serbs, 0; Biljaci [phoen], October 1995, Serbs, 0; Branesci, October 1995, Serbs, 0. Allow me to read wherever there is -- Bucesi [phoen], Svera [phoen], Breza, Donji Obrijez, all of these places number 0 Serbs, Donja Sumetlica, Donji Grahovljami, and further on is illegible. Then Gornji Grahovo, Jakovci, Koturici, Lipovac, Mali, Banovac, Mali Budici, Ozegovci, Popovci, Preko Praka, Prg Male [phoen], Ragule [phoen], Srednji Grahovo, Spanovica, Tisovac, Toranj Veliki, Banovac, Veliki Budic, and so on. So the number of the population in 1995, the number that was then, has been now reduced to a 0. Do you know anything about this? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 10937 to 10953

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that, and that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes. You say in those villages. But now we're giving you a total in the municipality of Pakrac. Before April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, do you want us to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would just like to ask the witness something, because I don't have two copies of this, and I need to ask him something, because this illustrates something that you do not understand, and it would be good for you to see so you could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A total of 16.300 citizens, the majority of that are Serbs, 7.806 are Serbs, 7.806. In that region, only 564 Serb citizens have remained in that whole area, so it has been cleansed 93 per cent. The remainder of the Serbs could be boiled down to a statistical error?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question to the witness. These are all assertions by you. Now, what area are you talking about, first of all? What area are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only talking about his municipality now, because I want to give you a clear example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, those are the -- just a moment. Let the witness deal with it, because it's his evidence that we're dealing with. You see the -- you remember the various figures that were put there. Can you assist us as to whether they're correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the numbers. They are correct. You talked about half the municipality, that there was 7.900. Well, no. In the municipality of Pakrac, there were about 14.000 Serbs, but in October 1995, there were 1.200 Serbs, because we did keep records of that in 1995. When you asked me specifically about the villages that you mentioned, and you asked me about ethnic cleansing, when you specifically asked me about the villages, I said that yes, there was ethnic cleansing specifically in those villages. So I didn't respond to something that you didn't ask me about. In the area of municipality of Pakrac, in those villages, ethnic cleansing was carried out. The number of Serbs was reduced to a minimum, houses were torched, their apartments were confiscated and they did not have any place to come back to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So 14.000 something Serbs. How many Serbs were there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. 14.600 or 14.800. And now you have 1.200.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In October 1995, there were 1.200. Now there are about 2.700 or 2.800.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they came back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's put these figures into perspective. 14.600 to 14.700 [as interpreted] and 1.200 indicates that, when you look at the municipality, ethnic cleansing was carried out to a degree of 93 per cent. There was only 7 or 8 per cent Serbs left. Now, when these people came back, it turns out that in 2002 the situation regarding ethnic cleansing in that area is still 80 per cent. So the number of people who returned are still fewer than 20 per cent of the Serb population that was there at that time. Is that so or not so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-037 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the stenographer is having problems and five minutes are necessary. Let me just look at our timing. We'll take a ten-minute break and reduce the breaks from then on. In fact, if we have a quarter-of-an-hour break now we can then sit until 1.00 thereafter. --- Break taken at 11.20 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before we lose the point, do you want the report, the Pakrac report that you referred to, the UN report, do you want that exhibited too?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you hand it in, please. Just a moment. We'll get a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit D43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's at the moment marked for identification. You said Prosecutor's Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D43. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have 50 minutes more for your cross-examination, and that will allow the other parties a few minutes to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will hurry. But before that, I would just like to clarify one question. You said that the witness, in principle, a witness in principle, and this one specifically, can talk about things that he took part in and that he has personal knowledge of, and I understand that. It is logical.
